summary: POC scoping focused on defining latency/throughput SLOs (TTFT vs TPOT), target p95/p99 numbers, workload sizing and measurement plan for a 3-week POC. Agreement to run synthetic + production-replay benchmarks; Redwood to provide harness and template, Praxis to provide traffic profiles and test environment access.
topics: Definition: TTFT vs TPOT vs overall TTF (time-to-first-token vs time-per-output-token)
Target SLOs: p95/p99 targets and acceptable error budget
Workload sizing: concurrency, token lengths, prefixes, KV/prefix cache
Benchmark types: synthetic, production replay, warm vs cold cache
Measurement & instrumentation: tracing, sampling, where to measure (edge vs model)
transcript: [00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I think we've got about 45 minutes. Maya from Redwood, Arjun our SE, thanks for being here.

[00:08] Liam O'Connor: Thanks Maya. Quick intro from our side - I'm Liam, CTO, Priya runs our ML team, Noah on infra, Zoe product. Our ask: we need a POC to validate latency SLOs for customer-facing assistants, and figure out costs at scale.
[00:22] Maya Chen: Great — goal for today is to align on success criteria, exact metrics (TTFT vs T-POT), workloads, and a measurement plan. Arjun will jump into the nitty-gritty.

[00:30] Arjun Patel: Cool. Quick definitions to make sure we're aligned: TTFT (time-to-first-token) = latency from request ingress to first token out; TPOT (time-per-output-token) — how long each subsequent token takes. Sometimes people call it per token throughput or T per token, so there's naming noise, but we'll use TTFT and TPOT here.
[00:50] Priya Rao: Sounds good. For our product, first token matters for perceived latency, but long responses also matter cause users stream. We care about p95 for TTFT and p99 for TPOT ideally.

[01:05] Arjun Patel: Typical pattern we see: set a hard p95 TTFT target (e.g., < 250 ms) and a p99 TPOT target (e.g., < 40 ms/token) for the primary assistant mode. But those numbers depend heavily on model size, quantization, and batch config.

[01:22] Noah Kim: Quick caveat - our front end does some prefetching and we have a mix of short prompts (~30 tokens) and long assistant outputs (~400 tokens) in production. We'll share the distribution.

[01:34] Maya Chen: Perfect — that distribution will determine effective batch sizes and KV cache hit rates. Two other scoping axes: concurrency (RPS/users) and cache warm vs cold. We should define tests for both.
[01:48] Priya Rao: We also have a high-sensitivity flow for paying customers with p95 TTFT < 150 ms if possible. That might push us to dedicated capacity or pinned models.

[02:00] Arjun Patel: Right — dedicated vs hosted is both cost and latency lever. For the POC we'll profile both a hosted Redwood run and a dedicated capacity run (if you want to spin one up) so you can see delta.
[02:12] Zoe Martinez: What's our measurement plan? Do you run synthetic or run against production replay?

[02:17] Arjun Patel: Both. Recommended plan: 1) Synthetic microbenchmarks to establish baseline TTFT/TPOT per model+hardware combo (cold start and warm), 2) Production replay using your real request traces to measure realistic p95/p99 with batching and cache behavior, 3) Live end-to-end measurement from browser to first token to validate client-side experience. We'll provide the harness.
[02:38] Liam O'Connor: For synthetic tests, how do you account for KV cache / prefix caching? Our assistants have long context and reuse lots of common system prompts.

[02:46] Arjun Patel: We simulate both cold (empty KV) and warm (pre-populated KV/prefix) runs. The harness lets you seed the KV cache with representative prefixes. Important: p95/p99 change significantly with cache hit rates.
[02:58] Priya Rao: On SLO numbers — you mentioned 250ms p95 TTFT, 40ms/token p99 TPOT. Are those realistic for a 13B model on A100 or do we need smaller models or quantized instances?

[03:08] Arjun Patel: On A100 GPUs, a quantized 13B with optimized kernels can hit ~200-300ms TTFT for short prompts in many configs. For p99 TPOT 40ms/token is achievable for batched throughput, but depends on batching window and sequence length. For strict 150ms p95 you likely need dedicated lower-latency instance types or model distillation/smaller model variants.
[03:28] Noah Kim: Our infra team will want concrete measurement points. Where should we instrument?

[03:34] Arjun Patel: Measure at three spots: 1) Client-side (browser/mobile) to capture perceived TTFT, 2) Ingress/edge timestamp to capture network+proxy latency up to Redwood, 3) Model runtime start/first-token and per-token timings. We'll provide tracing hooks and a small tracer shim.

[03:50] Maya Chen: Also add error budgets and success criteria: e.g., POC success = achieve p95 TTFT <= 250ms on production-replay for 95% of runs and p99 TPOT <= 50ms for streaming flows, or show a clear tradeoff and cost delta to reach 150ms p95.
[04:10] Priya Rao: That framing works. We want both the numbers and the cost to get there. Please include cost-per-1M-requests for each config.

[04:18] Arjun Patel: We'll include unit economics in the benchmark report: token cost, infra cost, amortized GPU hours for the POC scale. We'll run runs across model variants (7B/13B/30B / quantized), and config toggles (batching windows, KV caching, prefix caching, continuous batching).
[04:36] Zoe Martinez: Timeline?

[04:37] Maya Chen: Proposed: week 1 (this week) align and collect traces + set up test account; week 2 run synthetic baselines and warmups; week 3 run production-replay benchmarks + cost analysis; aim to deliver report by end of week 3. That's a 3-week POC.
[04:51] Liam O'Connor: Works for us, assuming we can get infra time. We'll prioritize providing the traffic CSV and sample vault of prompts.

[04:57] Arjun Patel: On sample sizes for p99 stability — we recommend at least 10k requests for each test configuration for stable p99, more for tail analysis. For p95 you can get reasonable estimates with fewer samples but p99 needs more data.
[05:09] Priya Rao: Good — we'll aim to give a week of traffic traces and a breakdown of short vs long. Also we'll note critical flows (signup flow, billing queries) that need stricter SLOs.

[05:18] Maya Chen: A couple of measurement notes: 1) Make sure the harness preserves original inter-arrival times for production replay to capture batching behavior; 2) Warm caches by replaying similar prefixes before measurement window; 3) Capture both throughput (RPS/tokens per second) and latency histograms (TTFT and per-token).
[05:36] Arjun Patel: Also include concurrency sweeps: run at 1x, 2x, 5x expected peak to understand degradation curves. We'll report throughput vs latency curves and where tail behaviour spikes.
[05:48] Noah Kim: Any constraints around security? We'll want SOC2 docs, SSO, VPC peering for private testing if needed.
[05:55] Maya Chen: We'll share SOC2 and security pack. For private testing we can set up a VPC endpoint or a short-lived dedicated environment. We'll list options in the kickoff doc.
[06:04] Zoe Martinez: What about measuring model-induced variability — like generation length variability causing p99 spikes?

[06:10] Arjun Patel: We'll stratify results by response length buckets (short <50 tokens, medium 50-200, long >200). That makes the tail drivers clear. Also include cold start distribution when models are evicted.
[06:22] Priya Rao: Are there recommended engineering knobs on our side to improve TTFT? We've got a front-end batching layer.

[06:28] Arjun Patel: Yes: early streaming from first-token, smaller request batching windows for low-latency flows, and prefix caching to reduce model compute for repeated system prompts. Also model quantization and reduced context length for some flows.

[06:40] Maya Chen: We'll include a short recommendations appendix in the report with levers: dedicated capacity, smaller/optimized models, reduced batch windows for low-latency routes, and caching strategies. We'll also show cost tradeoffs.
[06:50] Liam O'Connor: For acceptance criteria — recap please?

[06:53] Maya Chen: POC acceptance options: A) Achieve p95 TTFT <= 250ms and p99 TPOT <= 50ms on production-replay for key flows OR B) If not achievable, provide a clear path (config changes + cost) to meet stricter target like 150ms p95. Deliverables: benchmark report, scripts/harness, raw logs, and cost analysis.
[07:10] Priya Rao: Sounds good. Make sure the report has the raw histograms and the stratified buckets.

[07:15] Arjun Patel: Noted. We'll send the benchmark spreadsheet after this call — template includes columns for model, hardware, batch config, cache seed, sample size, and expected metric columns (TTFT p50/p95/p99, TPOT p50/p95/p99, RPS, tokens/sec, cost).
[07:28] Zoe Martinez: One more thing — can you show us sample dashboards? The ops team wants traceability to logs and per-route dashboards.

[07:34] Maya Chen: Yes we'll include a sample Redwood Console dashboard snapshot with per-route latency breakdown and trace links. We'll also include an example tracing span format so your infra can correlate.
[07:45] Liam O'Connor: OK let's call out owners and due dates.

[07:48] Maya Chen: Owner items — I'll send the spreadsheet and security docs (due 2027-10-22). Arjun will prep harness and scripts (due 2027-10-25). Priya will send traffic traces (due 2027-10-22). We'll aim to run the synthetic baseline early next week.
[08:05] Priya Rao: We'll also flag any red routes that need the stricter 150ms. I'll coordinate offline with Noah.
[08:10] Maya Chen: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with links to the benchmark doc and a calendar invite for the baseline run. Any last questions?
[08:17] Liam O'Connor: None from us, thanks. Looking forward to the report.
[08:20] Maya Chen: Thanks — talk soon. Bye.
[08:22] (call ends)
